article_title: A Key Immigration Ruling Is Flying Under The Radar
article_content:
Illegal immigrants have long used last-minute asylum claims to stall deportation, but a new court ruling could make that strategy much harder to pull off.
The decision, from the Fifth Circuit in Buenrostro Mendez v. Bondi, broadens who can be treated as an “arriving alien” under immigration law. That may sound technical, but the real-world effects are not.
The case itself concerned whether long‑term illegal aliens arrested inside the United States could seek immigration bond. But the court’s findings may have unintended consequences for a different group: aliens who use asylum filings to delay their inevitable deportation.
Under immigration law, arriving aliens follow a different process than other noncitizens. They are legally treated as if they are seeking admission at a port of entry, even if they are actually encountered inside the United States. When apprehended, they are expected to request asylum outright or at least say they fear persecution if returned home. If they claim credible fear, they are referred to an asylum officer for a Credible Fear Interview, or CFI. (RELATED: Trump Administration Shuts Down All Asylum Decisions Following National Guard Attack)
If they do not make that claim, they can be swiftly deported without ever appearing before an immigration judge. That is the system Congress put in place when it overhauled immigration law in 1996. But in practice, those rules have not always been applied consistently, especially in recent years. That inconsistency has helped fuel the massive backlog now choking the immigration system.
By contrast, aliens arrested further inside the United States generally enter full removal proceedings. Many file frivolous asylum applications not because they expect to win but to drag out their cases — sometimes for decades.
That problem has exploded in recent years. In fiscal year 2008 there were fewer than 14,000 defensive asylum requests. By FY 2024, nearly 1 million had been filed, and almost 2.5 million were pending. Many are submitted long after the one-year filing deadline and do not rely on changed conditions in the immigrant’s home country. They are filed by illegal immigrants who concede they are deportable and have no other legal way to stay.
The law treats arriving aliens differently for a reason. If they request asylum or express a fear of returning home, they are supposed to get a CFI immediately. Historically, about 80 percent of those who actually received a CFI passed that first screening. (RELATED: ICE Agents Arrive At US Airports Amid TSA Shortage As Democrats Keep DHS Shutdown Going)
But during the Biden-Harris years, many people described as “asylum seekers” were released without ever requesting asylum, claiming fear of persecution, or receiving a CFI. And many who did receive CFIs — especially as the border crisis worsened — were not found credible. Those two factors helped drive the wave of arrests made in the early months of the second Trump administration at immigration courts.
The statute is straightforward: arriving aliens who seek asylum are supposed to be screened immediately. If they fail that screening, they get one appeal. If that appeal is denied, they are to be deported.
This is where the Fifth Circuit’s ruling matters. By expanding who counts as an arriving alien, the court is effectively requiring some immigrants to raise asylum claims earlier than they currently do. That cuts directly into the strategy of filing defensive asylum applications years into a case simply to buy time.
Former INS official Dan Vara recounted a similar pattern that emerged in the 1990s. Haitians arriving in South Florida by boat were required to preview any asylum claim at the outset — a practice that developed in the wake of the Supreme Court’s 1993 decision in Sale v. Haitian Centers Council, Inc. The effect now would be the same as then: defensive asylum assertions — long used by long‑term illegal immigrant border crossers to buy time when they do not argue changed circumstances in their home country — will no longer serve that purpose. (RELATED: How Trump’s ICE Built Nationwide Police Alliance Right Under Democrats’ Noses)
If the Fifth Circuit’s interpretation is ultimately upheld — and there are already signs of resistance in some district courts both inside and outside the circuit — the biggest change will not be at the border. It will be inside immigration courts, where the long‑standing practice of former border crossers using defensive asylum filings to stall uncontested and inevitable deportations may finally come to an end.
